topic: question formation, including indirect questions and questions to the subject
rule_en: Standard questions invert the auxiliary and subject (What did she say?). Questions to the subject keep statement word order, since the question word IS the subject (Who said that?). Indirect questions (used inside a longer sentence for politeness) also keep statement word order and drop the auxiliary do/does/did.
structure: object question: QW + aux + subject + verb; subject question: QW + verb; indirect question: ...+ QW + subject + verb
examples_en: Who wrote this report?
Do you know who wrote this report?
What time does the meeting start?
Could you tell me what time the meeting starts?
Which company offered the best deal?
tip: In a subject question, never add do/does/did: 'Who called you?' not 'Who did call you?'.

options: Who broke the window?
Who did break the window?
Who did the window break?
questions.answer: Who broke the window?
questions.explanation: Subject questions keep statement word order, no extra auxiliary.

options: Can you tell me where the station is?
Can you tell me where is the station?
Can you tell me where does the station be?
questions.answer: Can you tell me where the station is?
questions.explanation: Indirect questions use statement word order.

options: What did she say to you?
What she said to you?
What said she to you?
questions.answer: What did she say to you?
questions.explanation: Object questions invert auxiliary and subject.

options: I wonder why he left so early.
I wonder why did he leave so early.
I wonder why he did leave so early.
questions.answer: I wonder why he left so early.
questions.explanation: Embedded questions drop the auxiliary do/did.

options: Which team won the tournament?
Which team did win the tournament?
Which team the tournament won?
questions.answer: Which team won the tournament?
questions.explanation: The question word is the subject, so no auxiliary is added.

options: Do you know what time it is?
Do you know what time is it?
Do you know what is the time?
questions.answer: Do you know what time it is?
questions.explanation: Indirect questions keep statement word order.

topic: emphatic auxiliary verbs; the...the... with comparatives
rule_en: Auxiliary verbs (do/does/did, or be) can be stressed to add emphasis or contradict something, even in positive sentences. The pattern 'the + comparative..., the + comparative...' links two changes that happen together, showing that one increases or decreases as the other does.
structure: I DO like it (emphatic); The + comparative + clause, the + comparative + clause
examples_en: I do understand your concern, but the decision is final.
She does work hard, whatever people say.
The more you practise, the more confident you'll become.
The earlier we leave, the less traffic we'll hit.
The harder the exam, the prouder I'll feel.
tip: In the 'the...the...' pattern, both clauses need a comparative form, even if it means using 'more' with an adjective.

questions.text: Choose the sentence with emphatic stress.
options: I do believe you, honestly.
I believe do you, honestly.
I am do believe you, honestly.
questions.answer: I do believe you, honestly.
questions.explanation: 'Do' before the verb adds emphasis.

options: The sooner we start, the sooner we'll finish.
The sooner we start, sooner we'll finish.
Sooner we start, the sooner we'll finish.
questions.answer: The sooner we start, the sooner we'll finish.
questions.explanation: Both clauses need 'the' + comparative.

options: The older he gets, the wiser he becomes.
The older he gets, wiser he becomes.
Older he gets, the wiser he becomes.
questions.answer: The older he gets, the wiser he becomes.
questions.explanation: Both parts of the pattern need 'the' + comparative form.

questions.text: Choose the sentence emphasising a contradiction.
options: She does care about the project, despite what you think.
She cares does about the project.
She is does care about the project.
questions.answer: She does care about the project, despite what you think.
questions.explanation: 'Does' + base verb emphasises the true statement.

options: The more expensive the hotel, the better the service.
More expensive the hotel, the better the service.
The more expensive hotel, better the service.
questions.answer: The more expensive the hotel, the better the service.
questions.explanation: Both clauses require 'the' + comparative form.

options: I did tell you, but you weren't listening.
I told did you, but you weren't listening.
I have did tell you, but you weren't listening.
questions.answer: I did tell you, but you weren't listening.
questions.explanation: 'Did' + base verb emphasises a past action.

topic: Present Perfect Simple and Continuous
rule_en: Use the present perfect simple to focus on the result or completion of an action, especially with quantities or a finished number of times. Use the present perfect continuous to focus on the duration or ongoing nature of an activity, often explaining a present situation.
structure: Simple: have/has + past participle (focus on result); Continuous: have/has + been + verb-ing (focus on duration)
examples_en: I've written three chapters so far.
I've been writing all afternoon, and I'm exhausted.
She's read that book twice.
She's been reading the same page for ten minutes.
How many emails have you sent today?
tip: With action verbs, both forms are often possible, but the continuous highlights duration and the simple highlights the finished result or quantity.

questions.text: Choose the sentence focusing on quantity.
options: I've read five books this month.
I've been reading five books this month.
I read five books this month, continuously.
questions.answer: I've read five books this month.
questions.explanation: A specific quantity uses the present perfect simple.

questions.text: Choose the sentence focusing on duration.
options: I've been working on this report all day.
I've worked on this report all day, finished.
I work on this report all day, currently.
questions.answer: I've been working on this report all day.
questions.explanation: Duration and ongoing effort use the present perfect continuous.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence explaining a present result.
options: Your eyes are red — have you been crying?
Your eyes are red — have you cried?
Your eyes are red — did you cry?
questions.answer: Your eyes are red — have you been crying?
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous explains a visible present result.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a finished number of times.
options: He's called me three times today.
He's been calling me three times today.
He called me three times today, so far.
questions.answer: He's called me three times today.
questions.explanation: A specific completed number uses the present perfect simple.

options: We've been waiting for over an hour.
We've waited for over an hour, currently.
We wait for over an hour, currently.
questions.answer: We've been waiting for over an hour.
questions.explanation: Emphasis on ongoing duration uses the continuous form.

options: She's finished the report already.
She's been finishing the report already.
She finished the report already, this moment.
questions.answer: She's finished the report already.
questions.explanation: Completion/result uses the present perfect simple.

topic: adjectives used as nouns; order of adjectives
rule_en: Some adjectives, preceded by 'the', can refer to a whole group of people sharing that quality (the elderly, the unemployed, the rich). These behave as plural nouns and take a plural verb. When several adjectives describe one noun, they usually follow an order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.
structure: the + adjective (= group of people, plural verb); opinion + size + age + shape + colour + origin + material + noun
examples_en: The elderly deserve more support from the government.
The unemployed are struggling to find new jobs.
She bought a beautiful small antique wooden box.
He wore an old, faded, blue cotton shirt.
The homeless need shelters, especially in winter.
tip: Adjectives referring to groups of people (the poor, the young) are always plural and never add -s themselves.

options: The rich often invest in property.
The rich often invests in property.
The riches often invest in property.
questions.answer: The rich often invest in property.
questions.explanation: 'The rich' is a plural group and takes a plural verb.

questions.text: Choose the sentence with correct adjective order.
options: She wore a lovely long red silk dress.
She wore a red long lovely silk dress.
She wore a silk red long lovely dress.
questions.answer: She wore a lovely long red silk dress.
questions.explanation: Order: opinion, size, colour, material.

options: The blind often develop a stronger sense of hearing.
The blinds often develop a stronger sense of hearing.
The blind often develops a stronger sense of hearing.
questions.answer: The blind often develop a stronger sense of hearing.
questions.explanation: 'The blind' is a plural group noun.

questions.text: Choose the sentence with correct adjective order.
options: He bought a beautiful old Italian leather bag.
He bought an Italian old beautiful leather bag.
He bought a leather beautiful old Italian bag.
questions.answer: He bought a beautiful old Italian leather bag.
questions.explanation: Order: opinion, age, origin, material.

options: The young are often more open to new technology.
The young is often more open to new technology.
The youngs are often more open to new technology.
questions.answer: The young are often more open to new technology.
questions.explanation: 'The young' is a plural group noun, plural verb.

questions.text: Choose the sentence with correct adjective order.
options: It was a fascinating tiny round wooden clock.
It was a round tiny fascinating wooden clock.
It was a wooden tiny fascinating round clock.
questions.answer: It was a fascinating tiny round wooden clock.
questions.explanation: Order: opinion, size, shape, material.

topic: narrative tenses, including Past Perfect Continuous; so/such...that
rule_en: Narrative tenses (past simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous) work together to tell a story clearly, showing background, sequence, and cause. Past Perfect Continuous emphasises how long something had been happening before another past event. 'So + adjective/adverb + that' and 'such + (a/an) + adjective + noun + that' introduce a result.
structure: had been + verb-ing (background duration before a past event); so + adj/adv + that; such (a/an) + adj + noun + that
examples_en: She had been working there for years before she finally got promoted.
It was so cold that the lake completely froze.
It was such a difficult exam that half the class failed.
He had been driving for six hours when the car broke down.
The film was so boring that we left halfway through.
tip: Use 'so' directly before an adjective or adverb, but 'such' before a noun phrase (with an adjective).

options: She had been studying for hours before the exam started.
She had studying for hours before the exam started.
She has been studying for hours before the exam started.
questions.answer: She had been studying for hours before the exam started.
questions.explanation: Past Perfect Continuous: had been + verb-ing.

options: It was such a good film that we watched it twice.
It was so good film that we watched it twice.
It was such good film that we watched it twice.
questions.answer: It was such a good film that we watched it twice.
questions.explanation: 'Such' + a/an + adjective + noun.

options: The traffic was so bad that we missed the flight.
The traffic was such bad that we missed the flight.
The traffic was so bad traffic that we missed the flight.
questions.answer: The traffic was so bad that we missed the flight.
questions.explanation: 'So' is used directly before an adjective.

options: He had been waiting for an hour when she finally arrived.
He waited for an hour when she finally arrived.
He has been waiting for an hour when she finally arrived.
questions.answer: He had been waiting for an hour when she finally arrived.
questions.explanation: Duration before another past event uses Past Perfect Continuous.

options: It was such an interesting story that nobody spoke.
It was so an interesting story that nobody spoke.
It was such interesting story that nobody spoke.
questions.answer: It was such an interesting story that nobody spoke.
questions.explanation: 'Such' + an + adjective + noun.

options: They had been arguing for weeks before they finally made up.
They argued for weeks before they finally made up, background.
They have been arguing for weeks before they finally made up.
questions.answer: They had been arguing for weeks before they finally made up.
questions.explanation: Background duration before a past event uses Past Perfect Continuous.

topic: position of adverbs and adverbial phrases
rule_en: Adverbs of manner usually go after the verb (or object); adverbs of frequency usually go before the main verb but after 'be'; adverbs of certainty (probably, definitely) usually go before the main verb; sentence adverbs (fortunately, surprisingly) usually go at the start of the sentence.
structure: subject + (frequency adverb) + verb + object + (manner adverb); Sentence adverb, + clause
examples_en: She speaks English fluently.
He's usually punctual for meetings.
I'll definitely call you tomorrow.
Fortunately, nobody was hurt in the accident.
She quietly closed the door behind her.
tip: Never place an adverb between a verb and its direct object: not 'She speaks fluently English', but 'She speaks English fluently'.

options: He carefully read every page of the contract.
He read carefully every page of the contract.
He read every carefully page of the contract.
questions.answer: He carefully read every page of the contract.
questions.explanation: Manner adverbs can go before the verb for emphasis, but never split the verb from its object.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence with a frequency adverb.
options: She's always late for work.
She always is late for work.
She is late always for work.
questions.answer: She's always late for work.
questions.explanation: Frequency adverbs go after 'be'.

options: He definitely knows the answer.
He knows definitely the answer.
He knows the answer definitely, always.
questions.answer: He definitely knows the answer.
questions.explanation: Certainty adverbs usually go before the main verb.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence with a sentence adverb.
options: Surprisingly, the team won the match.
The team, surprisingly won, the match.
The team won surprisingly the match.
questions.answer: Surprisingly, the team won the match.
questions.explanation: Sentence adverbs commenting on the whole sentence go at the start.

options: She explained the plan clearly.
She explained clearly the plan.
She clearly explained the plan clearly.
questions.answer: She explained the plan clearly.
questions.explanation: Manner adverbs go after the object, not between the verb and object.

options: I've never visited that museum.
I never have visited that museum.
I have visited never that museum.
questions.answer: I've never visited that museum.
questions.explanation: Frequency adverbs go after the auxiliary 'have'.

topic: Future Perfect and Future Continuous
rule_en: Use the Future Perfect for an action that will be completed before a specific point in the future. Use the Future Continuous for an action that will be in progress at a specific point in the future, or for a fixed, routine future arrangement.
structure: Future Perfect: will have + past participle; Future Continuous: will be + verb-ing
examples_en: By next year, I'll have finished my degree.
This time tomorrow, we'll be flying to London.
She'll have completed the project by Friday.
At noon, they'll be signing the contract.
By the time you arrive, I'll have cooked dinner.
tip: Future Perfect looks back from a future point ('will have finished'); Future Continuous is happening at that future point ('will be doing').

questions.text: Choose the correct Future Perfect sentence.
options: By 2030, scientists will have found a cure.
By 2030, scientists will finding a cure.
By 2030, scientists will be found a cure.
questions.answer: By 2030, scientists will have found a cure.
questions.explanation: Future Perfect: will have + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct Future Continuous sentence.
options: This time next week, I'll be lying on a beach.
This time next week, I'll have lying on a beach.
This time next week, I lie on a beach, then.
questions.answer: This time next week, I'll be lying on a beach.
questions.explanation: Future Continuous: will be + verb-ing.

options: She'll have graduated by the summer.
She'll be graduating by the summer, completed.
She'll graduate have by the summer.
questions.answer: She'll have graduated by the summer.
questions.explanation: Completion before a future point uses Future Perfect.

options: At eight o'clock, we'll be having dinner.
At eight o'clock, we'll have had dinner, in progress.
At eight o'clock, we have dinner, then.
questions.answer: At eight o'clock, we'll be having dinner.
questions.explanation: An action in progress at a future point uses Future Continuous.

options: By the time she arrives, we'll have left already.
By the time she arrives, we'll be leaving already.
By the time she arrives, we leave already, then.
questions.answer: By the time she arrives, we'll have left already.
questions.explanation: Completed before another future event — Future Perfect.

options: This time next month, I'll be living abroad.
This time next month, I'll have living abroad.
This time next month, I live abroad, then.
questions.answer: This time next month, I'll be living abroad.
questions.explanation: An ongoing situation at a specific future time uses Future Continuous.

topic: zero and first conditionals; future time clauses
rule_en: Use the zero conditional (if/when + present, present) for general truths and scientific facts. Use the first conditional (if + present, will + infinitive) for real future possibilities. Future time clauses with when, until, as soon as, before, after follow the same rule: present tense in the time clause, 'will' in the main clause.
structure: Zero: If/When + present, present; First: If + present, will + infinitive; When/Until/As soon as + present, will + infinitive
examples_en: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.
When the sun sets, the temperature drops quickly.
If it rains tomorrow, the match will be postponed.
I'll text you as soon as I land.
We won't leave until everyone is ready.
tip: Zero conditional describes something always true; first conditional describes one specific, realistic future possibility.

questions.text: Choose the correct zero conditional sentence.
options: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
If you mix red and blue, you will get purple.
If you mixed red and blue, you get purple.
questions.answer: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
questions.explanation: A general truth uses the zero conditional: present + present.

questions.text: Choose the correct first conditional sentence.
options: If she studies hard, she'll pass the exam.
If she studies hard, she passes the exam, will.
If she will study hard, she'll pass the exam.
questions.answer: If she studies hard, she'll pass the exam.
questions.explanation: A realistic future possibility uses present + will.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence with a future time clause.
options: I'll call you when I arrive.
I'll call you when I'll arrive.
I'll call you when I arrived.
questions.answer: I'll call you when I arrive.
questions.explanation: Present simple after 'when' referring to the future.

questions.text: Choose the correct scientific fact sentence.
options: Ice melts when the temperature rises above zero.
Ice will melt when the temperature rises above zero.
Ice melted when the temperature rises above zero.
questions.answer: Ice melts when the temperature rises above zero.
questions.explanation: A scientific fact uses the zero conditional.

options: We'll leave as soon as the taxi arrives.
We'll leave as soon as the taxi will arrive.
We leave as soon as the taxi arrives, will.
questions.answer: We'll leave as soon as the taxi arrives.
questions.explanation: Present simple after 'as soon as' for a future event.

options: If you don't water plants, they die.
If you don't water plants, they will die, generally.
If you won't water plants, they die.
questions.answer: If you don't water plants, they die.
questions.explanation: A general truth uses present + present, the zero conditional.

topic: unreal conditionals (mixed conditionals)
rule_en: Mixed conditionals combine a condition and result from different times: an unreal past condition can have a present result (if + past perfect, would + infinitive), or an unreal present condition can have a past result (if + past simple, would have + past participle).
structure: If + past perfect, ... would + infinitive (past condition, present result); If + past simple, ... would have + past participle (present condition, past result)
examples_en: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
If she weren't so shy, she would have applied for the job.
If he hadn't missed the train, he would be here by now.
If I were more organised, I wouldn't have forgotten the meeting.
If we had left earlier, we wouldn't be stuck in traffic now.
tip: Check the time of each clause separately — mixed conditionals often link a past action to a present state, or a present quality to a past event.

questions.text: Choose the correct mixed conditional sentence.
options: If I hadn't lost my job, I would have enough money now.
If I hadn't lost my job, I would have had enough money now.
If I didn't lose my job, I would have enough money now.
questions.answer: If I hadn't lost my job, I would have enough money now.
questions.explanation: Past condition (hadn't lost) with a present result (would have).

options: If she weren't so busy, she would have come to the party.
If she wasn't so busy, she would come to the party.
If she hadn't been so busy, she would come to the party, now.
questions.answer: If she weren't so busy, she would have come to the party.
questions.explanation: Present condition (weren't) with a past result (would have come).

options: If he had taken the job, he would be living in London now.
If he took the job, he would be living in London now.
If he had taken the job, he would have been living in London now.
questions.answer: If he had taken the job, he would be living in London now.
questions.explanation: Past condition (had taken) with a present result (would be living).

options: If I weren't so tired, I wouldn't have made that mistake.
If I wasn't so tired, I wouldn't make that mistake, then.
If I hadn't been so tired, I wouldn't make that mistake.
questions.answer: If I weren't so tired, I wouldn't have made that mistake.
questions.explanation: Present condition with a past result.

options: If they hadn't sold the house, they would still live there.
If they didn't sell the house, they would still live there.
If they hadn't sold the house, they would have still lived there.
questions.answer: If they hadn't sold the house, they would still live there.
questions.explanation: Past condition with a present result.

options: If I were better at cooking, I wouldn't have ordered takeaway last night.
If I was better at cooking, I wouldn't order takeaway last night.
If I had been better at cooking, I wouldn't order takeaway last night.
questions.answer: If I were better at cooking, I wouldn't have ordered takeaway last night.
questions.explanation: Present condition (were) with a past result (wouldn't have ordered).

topic: wish for present/future situations; wish for past regrets
rule_en: Use 'wish + past simple' for a present situation you want to be different. Use 'wish + would + infinitive' to express annoyance about someone else's present behaviour, or a wish for change in the future. Use 'wish + past perfect' to express regret about the past.
structure: wish + past simple (present); wish + would + infinitive (annoyance/future change); wish + past perfect (past regret)
examples_en: I wish I lived closer to my family.
I wish you wouldn't interrupt me all the time.
I wish I had studied harder at school.
She wishes she could speak more languages.
He wishes he hadn't said that to his friend.
tip: Never use 'wish + would' about yourself — use it only to talk about someone else's behaviour, or things you can't control.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a present wish.
options: I wish I had more free time.
I wish I have more free time.
I wish I will have more free time.
questions.answer: I wish I had more free time.
questions.explanation: Wish + past simple for a present situation.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence expressing annoyance.
options: I wish he would stop making so much noise.
I wish he stops making so much noise.
I wish he stopped making so much noise, right now.
questions.answer: I wish he would stop making so much noise.
questions.explanation: Wish + would expresses annoyance at someone's behaviour.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a past regret.
options: I wish I hadn't eaten so much at dinner.
I wish I didn't eat so much at dinner.
I wish I haven't eaten so much at dinner.
questions.answer: I wish I hadn't eaten so much at dinner.
questions.explanation: Wish + past perfect for a past regret.

options: She wishes she could travel more often.
She wishes she can travel more often.
She wishes she will travel more often.
questions.answer: She wishes she could travel more often.
questions.explanation: Wish + could for an ability you'd like in the present.

options: I wish I had taken that job offer.
I wish I took that job offer.
I wish I have taken that job offer.
questions.answer: I wish I had taken that job offer.
questions.explanation: Wish + past perfect for regret about the past.

options: I wish it would stop raining.
I wish it stops raining.
I wish it stopped raining, now, forever.
questions.answer: I wish it would stop raining.
questions.explanation: Wish + would for wanting a change in an ongoing situation.

topic: used to, be used to, get used to
rule_en: 'Used to + infinitive' describes a past habit or state that no longer happens. 'Be used to + gerund/noun' describes something familiar, not strange, in the present. 'Get used to + gerund/noun' describes the process of becoming familiar with something.
structure: used to + infinitive (past habit); be used to + -ing/noun (familiarity); get used to + -ing/noun (becoming familiar)
examples_en: I used to live in a small village.
I'm used to waking up early now.
It took months to get used to the new schedule.
She's used to working long hours.
We're slowly getting used to the cold winters here.
tip: 'Used to' talks only about the past; 'be/get used to' talks about familiarity in the present, not the past.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a past habit.
options: I used to play the guitar every evening.
I'm used to playing the guitar every evening.
I got used to playing the guitar every evening.
questions.answer: I used to play the guitar every evening.
questions.explanation: A discontinued past habit uses 'used to' + infinitive.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about present familiarity.
options: She's used to the noise from the street now.
She used to the noise from the street now.
She's getting used to the noise from the street, always.
questions.answer: She's used to the noise from the street now.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' describes present familiarity.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about becoming familiar.
options: It took a while to get used to driving on the left.
It took a while to used to driving on the left.
It took a while to use to driving on the left.
questions.answer: It took a while to get used to driving on the left.
questions.explanation: 'Get used to' describes the process of becoming familiar.

options: He used to smoke, but he quit years ago.
He's used to smoke, but he quit years ago.
He got used to smoke, but he quit years ago.
questions.answer: He used to smoke, but he quit years ago.
questions.explanation: A discontinued past habit uses 'used to'.

options: I'm still not used to this new keyboard.
I still don't use to this new keyboard.
I'm still not get used to this new keyboard.
questions.answer: I'm still not used to this new keyboard.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' describes present (un)familiarity.

options: They're slowly getting used to the time difference.
They slowly used to the time difference.
They slowly get used the time difference.
questions.answer: They're slowly getting used to the time difference.
questions.explanation: 'Getting used to' describes an ongoing adjustment process.

topic: gerunds and infinitives (advanced patterns, including verb + object + infinitive)
rule_en: Some verbs are followed by object + infinitive (want, ask, tell, expect, persuade). Some verbs change meaning depending on whether they're followed by a gerund or infinitive (remember, stop, try, forget). Some verbs are followed by a gerund even with a possessive or object pronoun (mind, imagine).
structure: verb + object + to-infinitive; verb + gerund / verb + infinitive (meaning changes); verb + possessive/object + gerund
examples_en: She persuaded him to apply for the job.
I remember locking the door before we left.
Please remember to lock the door tonight.
He stopped smoking last year.
Do you mind me opening the window?
tip: 'Remember + gerund' looks back at a memory; 'remember + infinitive' is a reminder about something not yet done.

options: They persuaded her to join the team.
They persuaded her joining the team.
They persuaded her join the team.
questions.answer: They persuaded her to join the team.
questions.explanation: 'Persuade' takes object + to-infinitive.

questions.text: Choose the sentence meaning he has a memory of doing it.
options: He remembers meeting her at the conference.
He remembers to meet her at the conference.
He remembered meet her at the conference.
questions.answer: He remembers meeting her at the conference.
questions.explanation: 'Remember + gerund' refers to a memory of a past action.

questions.text: Choose the sentence meaning it's a reminder for the future.
options: Please remember to send the email.
Please remember sending the email.
Please remember send the email.
questions.answer: Please remember to send the email.
questions.explanation: 'Remember + infinitive' is a reminder about something not yet done.

options: Would you mind me asking a question?
Would you mind me to ask a question?
Would you mind I ask a question?
questions.answer: Would you mind me asking a question?
questions.explanation: 'Mind' is followed by a possessive/object + gerund.

options: He stopped to answer his phone.
He stopped answering his phone, in order to.
He stopped answer his phone.
questions.answer: He stopped to answer his phone.
questions.explanation: 'Stop + infinitive' means he paused an activity in order to do something else.

options: They expect us to arrive by noon.
They expect us arriving by noon.
They expect we arrive by noon.
questions.answer: They expect us to arrive by noon.
questions.explanation: 'Expect' takes object + to-infinitive.

topic: past modals of deduction and preference: must have..., would rather
rule_en: Use 'must/can't/might have + past participle' for deductions about the past. Use 'would rather + past simple' to express a preference about someone else's actions (or a hypothetical alternative), and 'would rather + bare infinitive' for your own preference between actions.
structure: must/can't/might + have + past participle; would rather + bare infinitive; would rather + subject + past simple
examples_en: She must have left already; her coat is gone.
He can't have finished, it's only been ten minutes.
I'd rather stay home tonight than go out.
I'd rather you didn't tell anyone about this.
They might have missed the announcement.
tip: 'Would rather you + past simple' expresses a preference about another person's action, even though it refers to the present or future.

options: They must have taken the wrong turn.
They must taken the wrong turn.
They must have take the wrong turn.
questions.answer: They must have taken the wrong turn.
questions.explanation: Past deduction: must + have + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct negative past deduction.
options: She can't have forgotten our meeting.
She mustn't have forgotten our meeting.
She can't forgotten our meeting.
questions.answer: She can't have forgotten our meeting.
questions.explanation: Strong negative deduction about the past uses 'can't have'.

options: I'd rather walk than take the bus.
I'd rather to walk than take the bus.
I'd rather walking than take the bus.
questions.answer: I'd rather walk than take the bus.
questions.explanation: 'Would rather' takes the bare infinitive for your own preference.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about someone else's action.
options: I'd rather you called me tomorrow instead.
I'd rather you call me tomorrow instead.
I'd rather you to call me tomorrow instead.
questions.answer: I'd rather you called me tomorrow instead.
questions.explanation: 'Would rather + subject + past simple' expresses a preference about someone else.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about an uncertain past event.
options: They might have already left the party.
They might already left the party.
They might have already leave the party.
questions.answer: They might have already left the party.
questions.explanation: Uncertain past deduction: might + have + past participle.

options: He must have been very tired after the flight.
He must been very tired after the flight.
He must have very tired after the flight.
questions.answer: He must have been very tired after the flight.
questions.explanation: Past deduction with 'be': must + have + been + adjective.

topic: verbs of the senses
rule_en: Verbs of the senses (look, sound, smell, taste, feel) are followed by an adjective, not an adverb, when describing a quality. They can be followed by 'like + noun' for comparisons, or 'as if/as though + clause' for descriptions that may not be true.
structure: verb of sense + adjective; verb of sense + like + noun; verb of sense + as if/as though + clause
examples_en: This cake tastes amazing.
That noise sounds like a car alarm.
She looks as if she hasn't slept.
The plan sounds reasonable to me.
It feels as though summer will never end.
tip: Never use an adverb after a sense verb describing a quality: not 'It smells badly', but 'It smells bad'.

options: This soup tastes delicious.
This soup tastes deliciously.
This soup is tasting delicious.
questions.answer: This soup tastes delicious.
questions.explanation: Sense verbs take an adjective, not an adverb.

options: That smells like fresh bread.
That smells as fresh bread.
That smells fresh bread like.
questions.answer: That smells like fresh bread.
questions.explanation: 'Like + noun' is used for comparisons after sense verbs.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence with 'as if'.
options: He looks as if he's seen a ghost.
He looks as if he seen a ghost.
He looks as if he has see a ghost.
questions.answer: He looks as if he's seen a ghost.
questions.explanation: 'As if' + clause with present perfect describes an appearance.

options: The plan sounds risky to me.
The plan sounds riskily to me.
The plan is sounding risky to me.
questions.answer: The plan sounds risky to me.
questions.explanation: Sense verbs take adjectives, describing a quality.

options: This jacket feels soft.
This jacket feels softly.
This jacket is feeling soft.
questions.answer: This jacket feels soft.
questions.explanation: 'Feel' + adjective describes a quality, not an adverb.

options: It feels as though nothing has changed here.
It feels as though nothing changed here, ongoing.
It feels as if nothing change here.
questions.answer: It feels as though nothing has changed here.
questions.explanation: 'As though' + clause describes an impression.

topic: the passive (all forms); have/get something done; it is said that...
rule_en: 'Have/get something done' means arranging for someone else to do something for you. 'It is said/believed/thought that...' is an impersonal passive structure used to report general opinions or unconfirmed information without naming the source.
structure: have/get + object + past participle; It is said/believed/thought + that + clause; subject + is said/believed + to + infinitive
examples_en: We had our roof repaired last month.
She's getting her hair cut this afternoon.
It is said that the building is haunted.
He is believed to have left the country.
They're having the house painted next week.
tip: 'Have something done' focuses on the result and who arranged it, not who actually performed the action.

questions.text: Choose the correct 'have something done' sentence.
options: I had my car repaired yesterday.
I had my car repair yesterday.
I had repaired my car yesterday, by myself.
questions.answer: I had my car repaired yesterday.
questions.explanation: Have + object + past participle: someone else did it for you.

questions.text: Choose the correct impersonal passive sentence.
options: It is said that he speaks five languages.
It says that he speaks five languages.
It is saying that he speaks five languages.
questions.answer: It is said that he speaks five languages.
questions.explanation: 'It is said that...' reports unconfirmed general information.

options: She's getting her dress altered for the wedding.
She's getting alter her dress for the wedding.
She's getting altered her dress for the wedding.
questions.answer: She's getting her dress altered for the wedding.
questions.explanation: Get + object + past participle.

options: He is thought to be one of the richest men alive.
He is thought be one of the richest men alive.
He thinks to be one of the richest men alive.
questions.answer: He is thought to be one of the richest men alive.
questions.explanation: Subject + is thought + to + infinitive is a common impersonal passive pattern.

options: We're having the kitchen renovated next month.
We're having renovate the kitchen next month.
We're having renovated the kitchen next month, by us.
questions.answer: We're having the kitchen renovated next month.
questions.explanation: Have + object + past participle for something arranged.

options: It is believed that the treasure was never found.
It believes that the treasure was never found.
It is believing that the treasure was never found.
questions.answer: It is believed that the treasure was never found.
questions.explanation: Impersonal passive reporting a general belief.

topic: reporting verbs
rule_en: Reporting verbs (suggest, admit, deny, insist, warn, advise, refuse, threaten) each carry a specific structure and shade of meaning, more precise than simple 'say' or 'tell'. Learning the correct pattern for each verb (+ gerund, + to-infinitive, + that-clause, or + object + to-infinitive) makes reported speech far more natural.
structure: suggest + gerund/that-clause; admit/deny + gerund; insist + that-clause; warn/advise + object + to-infinitive/that-clause; refuse + to-infinitive; threaten + to-infinitive
examples_en: She suggested meeting earlier next time.
He admitted breaking the vase.
She denied taking the money.
He insisted that everyone stay for dinner.
The doctor advised him to rest for a week.
tip: Check each reporting verb's pattern individually — 'suggest' never takes object + infinitive (not 'suggested me to go'), while 'advise' does.

options: She suggested going to the cinema.
She suggested to go to the cinema.
She suggested me to go to the cinema.
questions.answer: She suggested going to the cinema.
questions.explanation: 'Suggest' is followed by a gerund or a that-clause, never object + infinitive.

options: He admitted making a mistake.
He admitted to make a mistake.
He admitted make a mistake.
questions.answer: He admitted making a mistake.
questions.explanation: 'Admit' is followed by a gerund.

options: The lawyer advised her to stay silent.
The lawyer advised her staying silent.
The lawyer advised to her stay silent.
questions.answer: The lawyer advised her to stay silent.
questions.explanation: 'Advise' takes object + to-infinitive.

options: He denied stealing the documents.
He denied to steal the documents.
He denied steal the documents.
questions.answer: He denied stealing the documents.
questions.explanation: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund.

options: She refused to sign the contract.
She refused signing the contract.
She refused sign the contract.
questions.answer: She refused to sign the contract.
questions.explanation: 'Refuse' is followed by the to-infinitive.

options: He warned us not to be late.
He warned us to not be late.
He warned us not being late.
questions.answer: He warned us not to be late.
questions.explanation: 'Warn' takes object + not + to-infinitive for a negative warning.

topic: clauses of concession and purpose
rule_en: Clauses of concession (although, even though, despite, in spite of) show a contrast between two facts. Clauses of purpose (to, in order to, so that, so as to) explain the reason for an action. 'Despite/in spite of' are followed by a noun or gerund, not a clause.
structure: Although/Even though + clause, ... ; Despite/In spite of + noun/gerund, ... ; ... so that/in order to + clause
examples_en: Although it was raining, they went for a walk.
Despite the heavy traffic, we arrived on time.
She left early so that she wouldn't miss the train.
He studied hard in order to pass the exam.
In spite of feeling nervous, she gave a great presentation.
tip: 'Despite' and 'in spite of' are followed by a noun or -ing form, never by a clause with a subject and verb — for that, use 'although' or 'even though'.

options: Although he was tired, he finished the marathon.
Despite he was tired, he finished the marathon.
In spite he was tired, he finished the marathon.
questions.answer: Although he was tired, he finished the marathon.
questions.explanation: 'Although' is followed by a full clause.

options: Despite the rain, the match continued.
Despite it rained, the match continued.
Although the rain, the match continued.
questions.answer: Despite the rain, the match continued.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun, not a clause.

options: She whispered so that nobody would hear.
She whispered so as nobody would hear.
She whispered in order nobody would hear.
questions.answer: She whispered so that nobody would hear.
questions.explanation: 'So that' introduces a purpose clause with a subject and verb.

options: In spite of losing the first game, they won the tournament.
In spite of they lost the first game, they won the tournament.
Despite they lost the first game, they won the tournament.
questions.answer: In spite of losing the first game, they won the tournament.
questions.explanation: 'In spite of' is followed by a gerund, not a clause.

options: He left early in order to catch the first train.
He left early so as catch the first train.
He left early for catch the first train.
questions.answer: He left early in order to catch the first train.
questions.explanation: 'In order to' + infinitive expresses purpose.

options: Even though she was exhausted, she kept working.
Despite she was exhausted, she kept working.
In spite she was exhausted, she kept working.
questions.answer: Even though she was exhausted, she kept working.
questions.explanation: 'Even though' is followed by a full clause.

topic: uncountable and plural nouns
rule_en: Some nouns are always uncountable in English even though their translation may be countable in other languages (advice, information, furniture, news, luggage). Some nouns are always plural and take a plural verb, with no singular form (clothes, scissors, trousers, glasses).
structure: a piece of + uncountable noun; uncountable noun + singular verb; plural-only noun + plural verb
examples_en: She gave me some useful advice.
I need a piece of information about the schedule.
My luggage is still at the airport.
These trousers are too long for me.
Where are my glasses? I can't find them anywhere.
tip: To count an uncountable noun, use 'a piece/item of...': a piece of advice, an item of furniture, not 'an advice'.

options: I need some information about the flight.
I need some informations about the flight.
I need an information about the flight.
questions.answer: I need some information about the flight.
questions.explanation: 'Information' is always uncountable, no plural form.

options: My scissors are in the top drawer.
My scissors is in the top drawer.
My scissor is in the top drawer.
questions.answer: My scissors are in the top drawer.
questions.explanation: 'Scissors' is a plural-only noun, taking a plural verb.

options: Can you give me a piece of advice?
Can you give me an advice?
Can you give me some advices?
questions.answer: Can you give me a piece of advice?
questions.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable; use 'a piece of' to count it.

options: The furniture in this flat looks new.
The furnitures in this flat look new.
The furniture in this flat look new.
questions.answer: The furniture in this flat looks new.
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

options: Where are my glasses?
Where is my glasses?
Where are my glass?
questions.answer: Where are my glasses?
questions.explanation: 'Glasses' (spectacles) is plural-only, plural verb.

options: The news was surprising this morning.
The news were surprising this morning.
The news are surprising this morning.
questions.answer: The news was surprising this morning.
questions.explanation: 'News' looks plural but is always uncountable, singular verb.

topic: quantifiers: all, every, both, and related expressions
rule_en: 'All' and 'every' both express totality, but 'every' is followed by a singular noun, while 'all' is followed by a plural or uncountable noun. 'Both' refers specifically to two people or things. 'All of/both of/none of' are used before pronouns and determiners.
structure: every + singular noun; all + plural/uncountable noun; both + plural noun (two items); all of/both of/none of + the/pronoun
examples_en: Every student must submit the form by Friday.
All students received the same instructions.
Both candidates performed well in the interview.
All of the tickets have already sold out.
None of us expected the announcement.
tip: 'Every' always takes a singular verb, even though it refers to a whole group: 'Every student has to attend', not 'have to attend'.

options: Every employee has received the new handbook.
Every employees have received the new handbook.
All employee has received the new handbook.
questions.answer: Every employee has received the new handbook.
questions.explanation: 'Every' + singular noun + singular verb.

options: Both of the answers were correct.
Both of the answer were correct.
Both the answers was correct.
questions.answer: Both of the answers were correct.
questions.explanation: 'Both of' + plural noun + plural verb.

options: All the information was useful.
All the informations were useful.
Every the information was useful.
questions.answer: All the information was useful.
questions.explanation: 'All' + uncountable noun + singular verb.

options: None of us were ready for the news.
None of we were ready for the news.
None us were ready for the news.
questions.answer: None of us were ready for the news.
questions.explanation: 'None of' + object pronoun.

options: Every one of the rooms was fully booked.
Every one of the rooms were fully booked.
All one of the rooms was fully booked.
questions.answer: Every one of the rooms was fully booked.
questions.explanation: 'Every one of' + plural noun still takes a singular verb.

options: Both my parents work in education.
Both of my parent work in education.
Every my parent works in education.
questions.answer: Both my parents work in education.
questions.explanation: 'Both' + plural noun (two people) + plural verb.

topic: articles (advanced uses)
rule_en: Beyond the basic rules, articles have special uses: 'the' with superlatives and unique institutions (the internet, the government); no article with most meals, means of transport (by car) and abstract nouns in general statements; 'a/an' in certain fixed expressions of rate (twice a week, $10 an hour).
structure: the + superlative/unique institution; Ø + meal/by+transport/abstract noun (general); a/an + expression of rate
examples_en: This is the best decision I've ever made.
We usually have dinner at eight.
She travels to work by bus every day.
He earns fifteen dollars an hour.
The government announced new regulations today.
tip: Learn fixed exceptions individually — articles with abstract nouns and institutions don't always follow the basic first-mention/unique rule.

options: This is the most difficult exam I've ever taken.
This is most difficult exam I've ever taken.
This is a most difficult exam I've ever taken.
questions.answer: This is the most difficult exam I've ever taken.
questions.explanation: Superlatives take 'the'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a meal.
options: We have lunch at one o'clock every day.
We have the lunch at one o'clock every day.
We have a lunch at one o'clock every day.
questions.answer: We have lunch at one o'clock every day.
questions.explanation: Meals generally take no article.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about transport.
options: She goes to work by train.
She goes to work by the train.
She goes to work by a train.
questions.answer: She goes to work by train.
questions.explanation: 'By' + means of transport takes no article.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence with a rate expression.
options: He visits his parents twice a month.
He visits his parents twice the month.
He visits his parents twice month.
questions.answer: He visits his parents twice a month.
questions.explanation: Rate expressions use 'a/an'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a unique institution.
options: The internet has changed how we communicate.
Internet has changed how we communicate.
An internet has changed how we communicate.
questions.answer: The internet has changed how we communicate.
questions.explanation: Unique institutions like 'the internet' take 'the'.

options: The government raised taxes this year.
Government raised taxes this year.
A government raised taxes this year.
questions.answer: The government raised taxes this year.
questions.explanation: 'The government' refers to a specific, known institution.
